extracted.intended_audience: writers submitting to or interested in The Paris Review; literary readers and contributors
extracted.subtask_description: The Paris Review's editorial mission describing what kinds of work it seeks and how it curates material (emphasis, selection preferences, and interview practice). Useful for writers aiming to submit or understand the magazine's priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on original creative work (fiction and poetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Paris Review hopes to emphasize creative work—fiction and poetry—not to the exclusion of criticism, but with the aim in mind of merely removing criticism from the dominating place it holds in most literary magazines and putting it pretty much where it belongs, i.e., somewhere near the back of the book.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority is given to original fiction and poetry. Criticism is acceptable but should not dominate the magazine; editorial placement and emphasis should foreground creative work over criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select for literary quality — 'good writers and good poets'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Review should “welcome these people into its pages: the good writers and good poets… So long as they're good.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary selection criterion is quality of writing. The magazine looks for work that demonstrates strong literary merit rather than notoriety, topicality, or sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid polemical/agitational voices — 'non-drumbeaters and non-axe-grinders'
rubrics_metrics.description: The founding mission states it should welcome “the non-drumbeaters and non-axe-grinders.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions that are primarily polemical, agitational, or stridently campaign-like are discouraged. Preferred pieces are literary in purpose and tone rather than agitation-driven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discover and introduce important/new writers
rubrics_metrics.description: “Decade after decade, the Review has introduced the important writers of the day.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial practice favors publishing emerging or early-career work that shows promise of lasting importance; historical examples (Adrienne Rich, Philip Roth, Italo Calvino, etc.) illustrate the magazine's track record and willingness to publish early or debut pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish selections and early appearances of significant works
rubrics_metrics.description: The magazine historically published important milestones and early appearances (e.g., selections from Beckett's Molloy, Kerouac's 'The Mexican Girl', early excerpts and first publications of works later widely anthologized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Review accepts substantial creative pieces including selections/excerpts that may represent larger works, and it values early presentation of material that may later be considered canonical.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-depth author interviews that let writers discuss life and craft
rubrics_metrics.description: “Letting the authors talk about their work themselves. The Review’s Writers at Work interview series offers authors a rare opportunity to discuss their life and art at length; they have responded with some of the most revealing self-portraits in literature.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews should be substantial, allowing authors to reflect at length on process, life, and craft. The magazine values revealing, wide-ranging conversations rather than short promotional Q&As; past interviewees (Faulkner, Nabokov, Didion, etc.) exemplify the intended depth and seriousness.
